content: The Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) ensures the validity and consistency of health content by aligning it with the Digital Tracking and Decision Support (DTDS) system. This process requires collaboration between health program managers responsible for family planning and their counterparts in digital health and health information systems. While each DAK focuses on a specific health program area, such as family planning, the kits are designed to be modular and can integrate with other health program areas within primary healthcare settings to promote service integration. Scenario 1: Incorporating WHO Guidelines into Existing DTDS Systems Countries with existing digital systems, such as electronic medical records (EMRs) and decision-support tools, can use the DAK to verify that the underlying content and data for specific health program areas align with WHO guidelines. Health program managers and implementers can extract specific decision algorithms from the DAK to incorporate into their systems. By systematically reviewing this documentation, they can identify differences in workflows, data inputs, and decision-support logic, understand the rationale for deviations, and adapt guideline content to local contexts. Scenario 2: Transitioning from Paper-Based to DTDS Systems For countries transitioning from paper-based systems to digital systems, the DAK serves as a starting point to streamline necessary data elements and decision-support features for optimized client-level digital systems. Users can cross-reference paper-based tools to identify missing fields or content that should be included in the digital system. Additionally, the WHO Handbook for digitizing primary healthcare provides stepwise guidance on mapping data from paper forms to digital systems, addressing redundant or non-value-adding data elements. Scenario 3: Linking Aggregate Reporting Systems to Point-of-Care DTDS Systems In some cases, countries may have digital systems for aggregate reporting and health management information systems (HMIS) but lack digital systems functioning at the service delivery level (e.g., community or facility level). The DAK includes aggregate indicators derived from individual-level data to bridge these levels. Tools like the WHO SCORE framework can support the use of routine data at facility and district management levels. Scenario 4: Leveraging Data Standards for Interoperability and Integrated Systems The DAK incorporates data elements mapped to ICD codes and other standards to facilitate the design of interoperable systems. The data dictionary in Web Annex A provides necessary codes for various data elements, reducing the time required for implementers to integrate global standards into their digital systems. Engaging clients in service delivery, such as transmitting health information, reminders, and feedback, accessing medical records, and self-monitoring health data, is a critical component of digital health systems. Content requirements for client-facing digital tools will be included in a forthcoming self-care interventions DAK. Linkages to the Broader Digital Health Ecosystem DAKs are part of a broader digital health ecosystem and should be used within the context of a strategic vision for DTDS systems, as outlined by the Ministry of Health (MOH). In the absence of such a vision, users should consult resources like the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, WHO guidelines on digital interventions for health system strengthening, and the WHO digital investment and implementation guide to select and apply appropriate digital health interventions. Health Interventions and Recommendations for Family Planning The DAK for family planning focuses on interventions and recommendations related to contraception, based on the WHO Universal Health Coverage (UHC) list of essential interventions. Key interventions include: Screening, testing, and counseling for contraceptive methods, including HIV testing, pregnancy screening, and medical eligibility assessments. Management of family planning and contraception, including assessing patient values and barriers, counseling on available contraceptive methods (e.g., hormonal, non-hormonal, long-acting, sterilization), and obtaining consent for procedures. Provision of contraceptive methods such as male and female condoms, hormonal and non-hormonal methods, intrauterine devices (IUDs), subdermal implants, sterilization, vasectomy, oral antiretrovirals for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and post-abortion or postpartum contraceptives. Removal of implants and IUDs, as well as monitoring follow-up visits. Care and support for survivors of intimate partner and sexual violence, including emergency contraception. WHO Guidelines and Recommendations The DAK reflects health recommendations and content published in WHO guidelines and guidance documents. These include the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, and guidance on contraceptive eligibility for women at high risk of HIV. Additional resources include the WHO Consolidated Guideline on Self-Care Interventions for Health and the WHO Recommendations on Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights. Personas in the Digital Adaptation Kit Personas represent relevant stakeholders or end-users of the system. For family planning, auxiliary nurse midwives and midwives are the primary personas for digital tracking and decision-support systems. These personas are based on WHO core competencies and credentials for health workers and require contextualization to meet the specific needs, motivations, and challenges of the targeted settings.
